abstract: Plasmodium falciparum parasites rapidly form thousands of infectious daughter cells, called sporozoites, within single oocysts during their development in the mosquito midgut. How parasites accurately compartmentalize these daughter cells remains poorly understood, mostly due to the exceedingly large oocyst volume (circa 113,000 m3 at the peak of sporozoite segmentation) and the substantial number of cells (5,000-10,000 sporozoites) hampering detailed ultrastructural studies. Here, we use a pre-commercial focused ion beam-scanning electron microscopy platform and custom-trained deep learning models to reconstruct at nanometer resolution the overarching cellular ultrastructure of two oocysts during mid- and late sporozoite formation. We unveil a highly synchronous segmentation process occurring with a striking degree of accuracy and reconstruct faithful stepwise interactions between key organelles in the different growth phases that likely ensure the fidelity of organellar segregation. We discover that sporozoites release membrane-bound cytoplasmic droplets, possibly to refine cell shape in preparation for their motility that drives transmission to humans. Contrary to previous assumptions, in both stages we conclusively visualize a single, interconnected sporoblast which we reason may help precisely coordinate signaling events that drive daughter cell formation. Our study provides foundational insight at unprecedented resolution into the ultrastructural features and changes characterizing the segmentation of P. falciparum sporozoites, conceivably the deadliest unicellular organisms in human history.
